summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base for managing physical topology identification and discovery. It lets network management tools learn how devices are physically connected.

eli5.summary: This gives network tools a way to ask which cable plugs into which device, so they can draw a map of the wiring.

questions: how to discover physical network connections
how do network tools discover physical connections
subtitle: A standard MIB for discovering which network cables connect which devices

tldr.problem: Network managers need a standard way to discover and report the physical connections between network devices, but existing MIBs do not provide a unified framework for this information.
tldr.mechanism: Define a Physical Topology MIB (PTOPO-MIB) that stores information about connections between ports on physical devices using standardized identifiers for chassis and ports, supporting both automated discovery and manual configuration.
tldr.outcome: Network management tools can query SNMP agents to learn the physical wiring of a network without vendor-specific tools, enabling multi-vendor interoperability for topology discovery.

today: RFC 2922 is an Informational document providing a standard MIB for physical topology discovery. It remains relevant for network management systems that need to discover and report physical connections in multi-vendor environments. The specification integrates with other standard MIBs, making it part of the larger SNMP management framework.

sections.title: The Need for Standardized Topology Discovery
sections.content:
Network devices such as switches, routers, hubs, and repeaters are physically connected by cables. To understand a network's structure, managers need to know which port on Device A connects to which port on Device B. Existing standards—the Entity MIB, Interfaces MIB, Bridge MIB, and Repeater MIB—each handle pieces of this information, but no single standard MIB provided a unified way to report physical connections.

RFC 2922 defines the Physical Topology MIB (PTOPO-MIB) to fill this gap. It provides a standard representation of physical topology connections, allowing different vendors' devices to report their physical connections in a way that management stations can understand and correlate.
sections.eli5: Different equipment makers were answering "which cable plugs in?" in different ways. This creates one standard answer so management tools from any company can understand the wiring.

sections.title: Physical Topology Concepts
sections.content:
The Physical Topology MIB uses a few core concepts. A chassis is a physical device (a router, switch, or hub). A port is a physical component that can connect to another port through a cable. A connection endpoint is a specific port on a specific chassis. A connection pairs two endpoints and represents the cable or circuit between them.

The MIB distinguishes between local and non-local connections. A local connection has at least one endpoint on the agent's own chassis (the device reporting the information); non-local connections have both endpoints somewhere else in the network.

Persistent identifiers are crucial. The MIB uses stable string-based identifiers (like serial numbers) rather than numeric indices that change after reboot, so connections remain meaningful across reboots and device replacements.
sections.eli5: A chassis is a box. A port is a plug. A connection is the cable between two plugs. The system remembers which cable is which even if you restart the device.

sections.title: Discovery Mechanisms
sections.content:
Devices discover physical topology using various methods. Active discovery involves sending topology protocol packets and noting which port they arrive on. Passive discovery observes traffic already on the network and builds a list of devices seen on each port.

Different media types have different discovery mechanisms. FDDI has a native topology protocol. Ethernet and Token Ring require passive listening or vendor-specific protocols. The PTOPO-MIB does not mandate a specific mechanism; instead it allows implementations to use any mechanism and report the results in a standard format.

Multiple mechanisms can coexist on a single network or even a single port, providing more robust topology information. The MIB records which discovery algorithm identified each connection, allowing managers to assess confidence in the information.
sections.eli5: Devices can learn about cables by listening to network traffic, by sending special test packets, or by asking other devices. The MIB lets them use any method and still report it the same way.

sections.title: MIB Structure and Objects
sections.content:
The PTOPO-MIB is organized into three main groups. The ptopoData group contains the ptopoConnTable, a table where each row represents one physical connection. Key columns identify the local and remote chassis and ports, the discovery algorithm used, the agent's network address, and the status of the connection.

The ptopoGeneral group contains scalar objects: a timestamp for the last change to the topology, counters for table inserts, deletes, drops (refused entries due to resource limits), and age-outs (entries removed because they became stale).

The ptopoConfig group allows managers to configure notification throttling (to avoid flooding with topology change traps) and hold times (how long to keep dynamic entries before removing them).
sections.eli5: The MIB has a table listing all the connections, some counters for how many connections were added or removed, and settings to control how often it sends update messages.

sections.title: Persistent Identifiers and MIB Relationships
sections.content:
The RFC requires agents to use persistent string-based identifiers for chassis and ports, drawn from the Entity MIB's entPhysicalAlias object or the Interfaces MIB's ifAlias object. This ensures that the same physical component is identified the same way across reboots.

The PTOPO-MIB integrates with other standard MIBs. Chassis and port entries link to Entity MIB components, interface information comes from the Interfaces MIB, bridge and repeater specifics come from the Bridge and Repeater MIBs, and address information may relate to RMON-2 address mappings.

Multiple identifier types are supported for flexibility: identifiers can be based on physical aliases, interface aliases, MAC addresses, or IP/other network addresses, allowing representation of connections even when standard aliases are not available.
sections.eli5: Each device and plug gets a name that stays the same, making it easy to trace which cable is which even after the device restarts.

sections.title: Notifications and Polling Efficiency
sections.content:
The PTOPO-MIB defines a ptopoConfigChange notification that fires whenever a connection is added, removed, or aged out. This allows network management stations to be alerted to topology changes instead of polling constantly.

Notification transmission can be throttled using ptopoConfigTrapInterval to prevent flooding the network with change notifications during unstable periods. Managers can also monitor ptopoLastChangeTime to verify they haven't missed notifications.

The design follows the principle of low polling impact: managers are notified of changes and can respond, rather than polling the topology table constantly. TimeFilter techniques from RMON-2 help management stations focus on recent changes.
sections.eli5: When the wiring changes, the device can send a message alerting management tools. This is better than having tools keep asking "did anything change?" all day long.
